meta.title: Who really said "Let them eat cake"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Marie Antoinette almost certainly never said it. The line first appears in Rousseau's Confessions (1782), pinned on an unnamed "great princess."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Let them eat cake'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Marie Antoinette. The line traces to Rousseau's Confessions (written 1765), attributed to an unnamed 'great princess' when she was a child in Austria.

answer.label: Not Marie Antoinette — first recorded by Rousseau
answer.authorDates: 1712–1778 · recorded the line; attributed it to an unnamed “great princess,” not Marie Antoinette
answer.sourceLine: The line first appears in Rousseau’s ‘‘Confessions’’ (Book VI, written 1765, published 1782), where he recalls “a great princess” who, told the peasants had no bread, said “Then let them eat brioche.” He never names her — and wrote it when Marie Antoinette was about nine years old and still living in Austria. There is no record that she ever said it; the words were pinned on her only in 1843, decades after her death.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from
source.excerpt: At length I recollected the thoughtless saying of a great princess, who, on being informed that the country people had no bread, replied, “Then let them eat brioche.”
trail: The phrase appears in Book VI of Rousseau’s Confessions, written in 1765 and published in 1782, attributed only to “a great princess” whom he does not name, per Wikipedia’s sourced account.
Rousseau wrote it when Marie Antoinette was about nine and still in Austria — she did not reach Versailles until 1770 — so she cannot be the “great princess,” as the chronology makes clear.
The words were first attached to Marie Antoinette in print by Alphonse Karr in Les Guêpes of March 1843, roughly fifty years after her death, according to Wikipedia.
source.excerptNote: Rousseau’s French reads “Qu’ils mangent de la brioche” — literally “let them eat brioche” (an enriched, buttery bread), traditionally Englished as “let them eat cake.” He calls the speaker only “une grande princesse” and gives no name.
source.rightsNote: The source work — Rousseau’s Confessions, published 1782 — and its long-standard English translations are centuries old and in the public domain in the United States. Note this concerns the text’s rights only; it does not make the popular attribution to Marie Antoinette correct.

author.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
author.heading: About Jean-Jacques Rousseau
author.bio: Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a Genevan-born philosopher whose writing on politics, education and the self helped shape the Enlightenment and the French Revolution. In Book VI of his posthumously published Confessions he records the “let them eat brioche” anecdote and credits it only to “a great princess” — a figure he names nowhere and may have invented. The line migrated onto Marie Antoinette generations later.

misattribution.heading: How it became a Marie Antoinette quote
misattribution.intro: “Let them eat cake” is one of history’s most durable misquotes — the wording, the attribution, and even the food are all shaky.

items.why: There is no record that Marie Antoinette ever said “Qu’ils mangent de la brioche.” The line predates her prominence: Rousseau put it in print by 1765, when she was a child in Austria, attributing it to an unnamed “great princess,” per Wikipedia.

The same story had earlier been told of other royals — two daughters of Louis XV (Mesdames Sophie and Victoire), and, a century before Antoinette, Maria Theresa, wife of Louis XIV — showing it was a floating anecdote, not a real quote, as Wikipedia notes.
The French is “brioche” — a rich, buttery bread — not gâteau/cake; the familiar English “cake” is a loose traditional rendering, per Britannica.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented source is Rousseau’s Confessions, which credits an unnamed “great princess” — not Marie Antoinette, who was tied to the line only in an 1843 magazine, fifty years after her death, per Wikipedia.

context.heading: Why the myth stuck
lead: The quote endures because it is a perfect political caricature: a pampered queen so detached that starvation strikes her as a menu problem. That image fit revolutionary propaganda against Marie Antoinette — already vilified as “Madame Déficit” — far better than the messy truth that the line was a stock anecdote decades older than her reign.

Rousseau himself treated it as hearsay, a “thoughtless saying” of some unnamed princess, and may have made it up. Only in 1843, well after both Rousseau and the queen were dead, did a French writer graft it onto Marie Antoinette — and it has never come off.
context.pull: Rousseau names no one; history supplied the name.
